title: What Citizenship Actually Asks of Us
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Schafer distinguishes between authority (power to control, command, decide) and leadership (capacity to create more truth, trust, care, and human possibility). Authoritarian energy consolidates power through fear and dominance; it does not heal civic life. When institutions weaken, the fantasy that they alone will sustain society dissolves, and the actual health of shared life depends on whether ordinary people become conscious participants. The antidote to authoritarian logic is not reaction or resistance alone but care—real care that disrupts indifference and helps people see themselves as bound together rather than arranged in hierarchy. Citizenship is active belonging, not passive observation: the recognition that your choices and care matter in shaping the tone and conditions of the places you inhabit. She asks what civic life requires: not endless vigilance performed as anxiety or victimhood, but the willingness to become trustworthy, to participate consciously, and to choose, again and again, in ways that strengthen rather than fray the fabric. Citizen leadership is rooted in how one chooses to belong—recognizing that true power lies in the capacity to create more truth and trust, not in the capacity to control.
points: Authority (power to direct) and leadership (capacity to create more truth and care) are distinct; authoritarian control produces reaction, not renewed civic health.
Civic renewal cannot be achieved solely through resistance; it requires construction of something new through the disruptive work of care and conscious participation.
Citizenship begins with belonging that takes responsibility: noticing, tending, and choosing repeatedly to help create conditions in which more life can flourish.
The capacity to create truth, trust, and care is a more reliable measure of leadership than formal authority or rank.
quotes: Authority and leadership are not the same thing. Authoritarian energy is not strong leadership. It is the impulse to control rather than uplift. To consolidate rather than cultivate. To choose fear over trust, domination over relationship, self-interest over the common good.

When systems weaken and trust is frayed, our relationship to one another matters more, not less. The fantasy that institutions alone will carry us dissolves. What becomes clear is that the health of shared life depends on whether ordinary people are willing to become more conscious participants.
Care is disruptive. It interrupts self-protection. It interrupts abstraction. It interrupts the habit of living as though other people's struggles and dignity are separate from our own.

Citizenship is not passive membership. It is active belonging. Participation. Stewardship. Care. The recognition that the places we live and the people we share them with are part of our moral and relational field.

True leadership is measured by the capacity to create more truth, more trust, more care, and more possibility for others.” Archived from Kathleen Schafer Substack (Extraordinarily Ordinary) on May 3, 2026 by Tim.
